lesson.title: How Wrong Is Close Enough: Measuring Linearization Error
lesson.summary: The gap between a true value and its linear approximation, error = f(x) minus L(x), grows with distance from a and depends on how sharply the curve bends away from its tangent line.
lesson.body:
Every approximation leaves something on the table, and linearization is no exception. Define the error as E(x) = f(x) - L(x), the difference between the actual value of the function and what the tangent line predicted. Understanding how E(x) behaves is what separates a useful estimate from a risky guess.

Two things control the size of that error. The first is distance: the farther x sits from a, the more room the curve has to peel away from the straight line that only matches it at a single point. The second is curvature, measured by the second derivative f''(a). If f is concave near a (f'' negative), the curve bends downward away from its tangent line, so the tangent line sits above the curve and linear approximation overestimates the true value. If f is convex (f'' positive), the curve bends upward away from the tangent line, which sits below the curve, and linear approximation underestimates.

Return to f(x) = sqrt(x) with a = 4, whose tangent line estimate for x = 4.1 was 2.025 against a true value of 2.024845673..., an error of about 0.000154. Because f''(x) = -1/(4x^(3/2)) is negative for sqrt(x), the function is concave, so that small positive error (estimate above truth) is exactly what the curvature predicts. Now push farther from a: at x = 5, the tangent line gives L(5) = 2 + 0.25(1) = 2.25, while the true value is sqrt(5) = 2.236068..., an error of about 0.013932. Moving ten times farther from a (a jump of 1 instead of 0.1) made the error roughly 90 times larger, not 10 times larger, which is the signature of an error that grows faster than distance itself, closer to the square of the distance.

The practical lesson is to always ask how far x is from a before trusting a linear estimate. Close in, the error is tiny and often negligible; farther out, it can grow quickly enough to make the approximation useless.
